p.src: Now when the generals had revived Song Jiang, it was a long while before he regained consciousness. He said to Wu Yong and the others, “This time we shall surely fail to subdue Fang La! Ever since we crossed the river, fortune has gone so badly that we have lost eight of our brothers in succession. …” Wu Yong urged him, “Commander, you must not speak so, lest you weaken the army’s spirit. When we defeated the Great Liao, every man, high and low, returned safely to the capital; that too was ordained by Heaven. That our brothers have fallen in this campaign is the allotted span of each man’s life. Plainly, since crossing the river we have taken three great prefectures in succession: Runzhou, Changzhou, and Xuanzhou. All this comes from the Son of Heaven’s boundless blessings and our commander’s awe-inspiring might. How can you call it ill fortune? Why should the Vanguard lose heart of his own accord?” Song Jiang said, “Even if our heavenly allotment is nearing its end, I think of how we one hundred and eight answered to the constellations above and accorded with what was written in the heavens, and how close my brothers are to me, like my own hands and feet. Hearing such dreadful news today, I cannot help but grieve.” Wu Yong again consoled him: “Commander, please cease your sorrow and do not harm your honored health. For now, please attend to deploying troops in support of the attack on Wuxi County.” Song Jiang said, “Have Master Chai remain here to keep me company. Write separate military orders and have Superintendent Dai deliver them for me. Reply to Vanguard Lu, ordering him to advance upon Huzhou and then come quickly to rendezvous at Hangzhou.” Wu Yong had Pei Xuan write the reply and military orders, then sent Dai Zong off to Xuanzhou. Of this, no more need be said.

p.src: Meanwhile, Lü Shinang fled back to Wuxi County with Xu Ding. There they met the relief force dispatched by the Third Prince of Suzhou. At its head was Wei Zhong, Commander of the Six Armies, who had brought more than ten staff officers and ten thousand troops to relieve Changzhou. The two forces joined and held Wuxi County. Privy Councillor Lü related how Jin Jie had surrendered the city. Wei Zhong said, “Set your mind at ease, Councillor. I shall assuredly recover Changzhou.” Just then a scout reported, “The Song army is near. Make ready at once!” Wei Zhong at once mounted and led his troops out of the north gate to meet the enemy. He soon saw that the Song host was overwhelming. At its head came “Black Whirlwind” Li Kui, leading Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun in a headlong charge. Wei Zhong’s courage failed him. Before his troops could even form ranks, they were routed and fled. As he hastily retreated into Wuxi County, the four warriors were already close behind his horse and pursued him into the county seat. Privy Councillor Lü fled through the south gate. Guan Sheng led in his troops and seized Wuxi County. Wei Zhong and Xu Ding likewise escaped through the south gate, and all returned to Suzhou. Having taken the county seat, Guan Sheng and the others immediately sent a man galloping to report to Vanguard Song. Song Jiang and all the chieftains came to Wuxi County. They issued proclamations to reassure the local people and restore their status as lawful subjects, then brought in the main army and quartered it throughout the county. They also sent a memorial requesting that Generals Zhang and Liu be assigned to guard Changzhou.

p.src: Now Privy Councillor Lü joined Wei Zhong and Xu Ding, and the three led their battered remnant troops back to Suzhou. They appealed to the Third Prince for aid, saying that the Song forces were too powerful to withstand and had swept down upon them, causing the city to fall. The Third Prince flew into a rage and ordered his guards to drag Privy Councillor Lü away, behead him, and report when it was done. Wei Zhong and the others pleaded, “The officers under Song Jiang command troops seasoned in war. Among them are many valiant heroes of extraordinary prowess; moreover, their foot soldiers are all underlings from Liangshan Marsh, most of them practiced fighters. That is why they are so difficult to oppose.” Fang Mao said, “For now I shall leave the stroke owed to your neck in abeyance. Take five thousand troops and ride out first to reconnoiter. I shall assign my generals and follow shortly to support you.” Lü Shinang bowed his thanks, donned his full armor, took up his eighteen-foot serpent spear, mounted, and led the troops out of the city first.

p.src: Thereupon the Third Prince, Fang Mao, donned his armor in person, took up a painted halberd, mounted, and rode out to battle, overseeing the troops of the central army as they advanced to fight. The eight great generals formed ranks before his horse. Behind him, twenty or thirty deputy commanders stood in perfect order, leading fifty thousand southern troops out through Changhe Gate to meet the Song army. In the vanguard, Lü Shinang, leading Wei Zhong and Xu Ding, had already passed Hanshan Temple and was advancing toward Wuxi County. Song Jiang had already learned of this through his scouts. He led out all his many principal and deputy commanders, deployed the army from Wuxi County, and advanced more than ten li. The two armies met, their banners and drums in sight of one another, and each drew up in battle array. Still smarting from his humiliation, Lü Shinang spurred his mount, leveled the spear in his hands, and rode out in person to challenge Song Jiang. Seeing him from beneath the commander’s banner, Song Jiang turned and asked, “Who dares capture this villain?” Before he had finished speaking, “Gold-Lancer” Xu Ning raised his golden spear, urged his horse into a gallop, and rode before the lines to engage Privy Councillor Lü. The two generals crossed weapons while both sides shouted encouragement. After more than twenty bouts, Lü Shinang left an opening, and Xu Ning thrust a spear into his ribs, knocking him from his horse. Both armies raised a tremendous shout. “Black Whirlwind” Li Kui brandished his twin axes; “God of Death” Bao Xu charged with his throwing sword; and Xiang Chong and Li Gun each flourished spear and shield as they stormed into the enemy lines, throwing the southern army into chaos.

p.src: Song Jiang drove his troops forward in pursuit and came face-to-face with Fang Mao’s main army. Both sides used volleys of arrows to hold the enemy at bay, then drew up their battle lines. Eight commanders formed a line before the southern army. In the central command, Fang Mao heard that Privy Councillor Lü had been slain. Enraged, he rode out with his halberd held crosswise and reviled Song Jiang: “You are nothing but a band of brigands from Liangshan Marsh who plunder homes and rob travellers. The Song must be nearing its fall indeed to appoint you vanguard and send you invading my lands! Today I shall exterminate every last one of you before I withdraw my troops!” Song Jiang pointed at him from horseback and replied: “You wretch are merely one of a band of rustics from Muzhou. What fortune or destiny could you possess, that you vainly aspire to found a royal hegemony? Surrender while there is still time, and I may spare your life! The armies of Heaven have reached this place, yet still you resist with specious words! I swear I shall not withdraw until I have destroyed you all!” Fang Mao shouted: “Enough of this war of words! I have eight fierce commanders here. Do you dare send out eight men to fight them?” Song Jiang laughed. “If two of my men were to face one of yours, they could hardly be called heroes. Send out your eight, and I shall send eight of my chief commanders. Let them match their skills and decide the victor. Whoever is struck from his horse shall be carried back by his own side. No one may wound another with a hidden arrow or seize the bodies of the fallen. If no victor emerges, neither army may join in a general melee; we shall arrange another contest tomorrow.” On hearing this, Fang Mao ordered his eight commanders forward. Each gripped his weapon and galloped to the front. Song Jiang said, “Let the mounted commanders have precedence in going forth to fight. …” Before he had finished speaking, eight commanders rode out together. They were Guan Sheng, Hua Rong, Xu Ning, Qin Ming, Zhu Tong, Huang Xin, Sun Li, and Hao Siwen. As the gate banners parted within Song Jiang’s lines, eight chief commanders emerged, four to either side. All spurred their horses together and rode straight to the field. Ornate drums thundered and many-coloured banners waved between the armies. Each side fired a signal cannon, and amid the battle cries of both hosts, all sixteen horsemen charged out, each sought an opponent, and the pairs fell to fighting. And how were those sixteen commanders matched when they found their opponents and crossed weapons? Guan Sheng fought Liu Yun; Qin Ming fought Zhang Wei; Hua Rong fought Xu Fang; Xu Ning fought Wu Fu; Zhu Tong fought Gou Zheng; Huang Xin fought Guo Shiguang; Sun Li fought Zhen Cheng; and Hao Siwen fought Chang Sheng. The spectacle truly defied both brush and picture. All that could be seen was this:

p.src: Battle dust billowed wildly; murderous fury filled the field. Each man longed to be a Nezha; every one vied to become a Jingde. Thirty-two arms shuttled to and fro like looms weaving brocade; Sixty-four hooves flew like wind-chasing hailstones. The standards intermingled until red, white, blue, and yellow could scarcely be distinguished; Weapons crossed until spear, sabre, sword, and halberd could no longer be told apart. Look upon them wheeling through the smoke of battle: they truly resembled revolving lanterns at the Lantern Festival.

p.src: The next day, when the southern troops did not emerge, Song Jiang took Hua Rong, Xu Ning, Huang Xin, and Sun Li, together with more than thirty cavalrymen, to reconnoitre the city. He saw that Suzhou was encircled on every side by waterways and that its walls were strong. He thought, “The city cannot be taken quickly.” He returned to camp and consulted Wu Yong about a plan for attacking the city. Someone reported: “Li Jun, a chief commander of the naval forces, has come from Jiangyin to see the commander-in-chief.” Song Jiang ordered that he be admitted to the command tent. When Li Jun entered, Song Jiang asked him for news from the coastal regions. Li Jun replied: “Since I was assigned command of the naval forces, Shi Xiu and the others and I have fought our way to Jiangyin, Taicang, and other places along the coast. The defending commander Yan Yong and his deputy Li Yu led their warships out to engage us. On his ship, Yan Yong was thrust into the water by a spear stroke from Ruan Xiao’er, while Li Yu was killed by a storm of arrows. Thus we captured Jiangyin and Taicang. At present Shi Xiu, Zhang Heng, and Zhang Shun have gone to take Jiading, while the three Ruan brothers have gone to take Changshu. I have come expressly to report our victory.” Song Jiang was delighted by the news. He rewarded Li Jun and ordered him to proceed to Changzhou, meet Pacification Commissioners Zhang and Liu, and submit a written report.

p.src: Li Jun went straight to Changzhou and met Pacification Commissioner Zhang and Commander Liu. He gave a full account of the recovery of Jiangyin, Taicang, and the coastal islands, and of the deaths of the rebel commanders Yan Yong and Li Yu. Pacification Commissioner Zhang granted him a reward and ordered him to return to Vanguard Commander Song and await deployment. Li Jun returned to the camp at Hanshan Temple and presented himself to Vanguard Commander Song. Since Song Jiang had observed the broad waters outside Suzhou and knew that ships and naval forces would be needed for the fighting, he kept Li Jun with him. He ordered him to muster and inspect the vessels in preparation for action. Li Jun said, “Allow me first to inspect the breadth and narrowness of the waterways and determine how our forces may be employed. Then we can decide what to do.” Song Jiang agreed. Li Jun was gone for two days. On returning, he reported: “Due south of the city lies Lake Tai. I would like a single boat prepared so that I may enter a small inlet at Yixing, slip secretly into Lake Tai, and make my way out through Wujiang to gather intelligence from the south. We can then advance, attack from all four sides, and take the city.” Song Jiang said, “Your proposal is excellent, brother, but there is no assistant available to accompany you.” He immediately assigned Squire Li, together with Kong Ming, Kong Liang, Shi En, and Du Xing, to go to Jiangyin, Taicang, Kunshan, Changshu, Jiading, and the other districts. They were to assist the naval forces in recovering the coastal county seats, thereby freeing Tong Wei and Tong Meng to return and aid Li Jun in his mission. Li Ying accepted the military orders, took leave of Song Jiang, and led the four subordinate commanders toward Jiangyin. Within two days, Tong Wei and Tong Meng returned and paid their respects to Vanguard Commander Song. After speaking reassuringly to them, Song Jiang ordered them to accompany Li Jun in a small boat and gather intelligence from the south.

p.src: Across the softly swelling waters white gulls fly; spring deepens in lucid green that might dye one’s robes. Men journey south and north and grow old, while the setting sun forever sees the fishing boats home.

p.src: Presently Li Jun, Tong Wei, Tong Meng, and the two boatmen set out in a small skiff, heading straight for Lake Tai. As they drew near Wujiang, they saw in the distance a fleet of some forty or fifty fishing boats. Li Jun said, “Let us pretend we have come to buy fish and go over there to make inquiries.” The five of them rowed straight up beside the fishing boats, and Li Jun called, “Old fisherman, have you any large carp?” A fisherman replied, “If you want large carp, follow me home and I will sell you some there.” Li Jun rowed after the fishing boats. Before long, they gradually approached a settlement. Looking around, they saw the place encircled by bent willows, with more than twenty households inside the hedges. The fisherman moored his boat first, then led Li Jun, Tong Wei, and Tong Meng ashore and into a manor compound. The moment they stepped through the gate, the man coughed once. Seven or eight burly fellows rushed out from both sides, all carrying hooked poles; they caught the three men at once and dragged them straight into the compound. Without asking them a single question, they bound all three to wooden posts. When Li Jun looked up, he saw four stalwart men seated in the thatched hall. The leader had a red beard and yellow hair and wore a blue silk-padded jacket. The second was tall and thin, with a short beard, and wore a dark green round-collared cotton robe. The third had a dark face and a long beard. The fourth had a bony face, broad cheeks, and a spreading ring of whiskers. Those last two both wore blue padded jackets of the same kind. Each wore a black felt hat, and weapons rested beside them all. The leader barked at Li Jun, “You wretches—where are you from? Just cut out their hearts and livers for us to eat with our wine.” Hearing this, Li Jun thought, “For many years I was a smuggler on the Xunyang River, and for several more I played the hero in the Marsh of Mount Liang, yet never did I imagine that today my life would end here! So be it, so be it, so be it!” He sighed, then looked at Tong Wei and Tong Meng and said, “Today I have dragged you two brothers down with me. If we become ghosts, at least we shall go together!” Tong Wei and Tong Meng said, “Brother, do not speak so. We are content even if we die. Our only regret is that dying here will bury your illustrious name in obscurity.” The three looked at one another, thrust out their chests, and prepared to die. Give us your names, so that we may know.” Li Jun replied, “If you mean to kill us, then kill us. We shall not tell you our names even at the point of death, only to invite the ridicule of you heroes!” At these words, the leader sprang to his feet, took a knife, cut through all their bonds, and released the three men. p.src: one Tong Wei, the ‘Cave-Emerging Jiao,’ and the other Tong Meng, the ‘River-Churning Sea Monster.’ We have now accepted the imperial amnesty. Having lately defeated the state of Liao and marched back toward the capital, we were again commanded by imperial decree to come and subdue Fang La. If you are men under Fang La, then escort the three of us away and claim your reward. Do not imagine that we will struggle!” When the four heard this, they bowed to the ground, knelt together, and cried, “We had eyes but failed to recognize Mount Tai. Our offense just now was grievous—please forgive us! Please forgive us! We four brothers are not Fang La’s men. We all formerly made our living among the outlaws of the greenwood. Later we found this place, called Elm-Willow Village, surrounded on all sides by deep channels that no one can enter without a boat. We four use the fishermen as our eyes and ears and seek our livelihood on Lake Tai. Over this past winter we have all learned something of the waterways, and so no one dares come near to molest us. We have long heard how Song Gongming of the Marsh of Mount Liang gathered heroes from across the realm, and we have heard your illustrious name as well. We also heard of a man called Zhang Shun, the ‘White Streak in the Waves.’ Never did we imagine we would meet you today, elder brother!” Li Jun said, “Zhang Shun is my brother and likewise a naval commander of the same rank. He is now in the Jiangyin region hunting down the rebels. Another day I shall bring him here to meet you. May I ask the illustrious names of you four?” The leader replied, “Since we younger brothers have traveled in the greenwood, each of us has an alias. Please do not laugh at us, elder brother! I am Fei Bao, the ‘Red-Whiskered Dragon’; the others are Ni Yun, the ‘Curly-Haired Tiger,’ Bu Qing, the ‘Jiao of Lake Tai,’ and Di Cheng, the ‘Lean-Faced Bear.’” On hearing the four names, Li Jun rejoiced and said, “From now on, gentlemen, let there be no suspicion between us. Happily, we are all one family! My elder brother Song Gongming now serves as chief vanguard in the campaign against Fang La. At present he means to take Suzhou, but matters are not proceeding smoothly, so he specially sent the three of us to scout the way. Now that we have met you four heroes, you may come with me to see our vanguard commander. He will secure official posts for you all, and once Fang La has been subdued, the court will promote and employ you.” Fei Bao said, “Allow me to answer: if we four had wanted to become officials, we could long ago have held command under Fang La. We have no wish for office; we seek only a free and happy life. If you need the help of us four, elder brother, we will go through water or fire for you. But if you speak of securing official posts for us, we truly do not want them.” Li Jun said, “If that is how you feel, then why do we not swear brotherhood together right here?” The four heroes were overjoyed at this. They had a pig and a sheep slaughtered, brought out wine and laid a feast, and swore brotherhood with Li Jun as their elder brother. Li Jun also had Tong Wei and Tong Meng join them in the oath of brotherhood.

p.src: The seven men held council at Willow Manor. They spoke of Song Gongming's plan to take Suzhou: “Fang Mao refuses to come out and fight, the city is surrounded by water, and there is no road by which to attack it. The waterways are too narrow for our boats to engage the enemy. How can we possibly break the city?” Fei Bao said, “Brother, set your mind at ease and stay here for two days. Men under Fang La often come from Hangzhou to Suzhou on official business. We can seize such an opportunity and take the city by stratagem. I shall send several fishermen to gather intelligence. If anyone comes, we will devise our plan.” Li Jun said, “An excellent idea!” Fei Bao summoned several fishermen and sent them ahead, while he and Li Jun remained at the manor drinking each day. After they had stayed there for two or three days, the fishermen returned and reported: “At Pingwang Town there are more than ten transport boats. A yellow flag flies at each stern, bearing the words ‘Armor and Garments Made for the Prince's Palace.’ They have plainly been sent from Hangzhou. There are only five to seven men aboard each boat.” Li Jun said, “Now that this opportunity has arisen, I earnestly ask you brothers to lend me your strength.” Fei Bao said, “We shall go at once.” Li Jun said, “But if even one man escapes from those boats, the plan will fail.” Fei Bao said, “Rest easy, brother. Leave it all to us.” They immediately assembled sixty or seventy small fishing boats. Each of the seven heroes took one boat, while the rest were manned by fishermen, all of whom concealed weapons about them. They passed through the narrow creeks into the great river, spread out, and went to intercept the convoy. That night the sky was filled with stars and moonlight, and the ten government boats lay moored before the Dragon King Temple east of the river. Fei Bao's boat arrived first. At a sudden signal from his whistle, the sixty or seventy fishing boats closed in together and grappled themselves to the large vessels. The men aboard the government boats scrambled out, but were promptly caught with grappling hooks and bound together in groups of three or five. Even those who managed to jump into the water were hooked and hauled aboard. They fastened their small boats to the government vessels and moved them all into the depths of Lake Tai. By the time they reached Willow Manor, it was already the fourth watch. They bound all the lesser men into a single chain, weighted them with great stones, and cast them into Lake Tai to drown. They captured the two leaders and questioned them. The men proved to be arsenal officials serving the Crown Prince of Fang La, Prince Nan'an Fang Tianding, who guarded Hangzhou. By special royal command, they were escorting three thousand newly finished suits of iron armor to Suzhou for delivery to the Third Prince, Fang Mao. Li Jun asked their names and took all their credentials and official documents, then killed the two arsenal officials as well. Li Jun said, “I must go in person to consult with our elder brother before we can carry out this undertaking.” Fei Bao said, “I will have men ferry you over. Going by the narrow waterways will bring you more quickly to the army.” He called two fishermen and had them row Li Jun away in a swift boat. Li Jun instructed Tong Wei, Tong Meng, Fei Bao, and the others to hide the boats carrying the garments and armor quietly in the inlet behind the manor and let no one discover them. Fei Bao said, “It shall be done.” He then set about arranging the boats.

p.src: Now Li Jun and the two fishermen set their light, swift boat in motion, took the narrow waterways directly, and rowed to the army, going ashore at Hanshan Temple. He entered the camp, met Commander Song, and related the whole affair in detail. Wu Yong was delighted when he heard it and said, “If that is so, Suzhou is ours for the taking! Have the commander issue orders at once. Send Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun with two hundred shield-bearing assault troops to follow Li Jun back to the manor by Lake Tai. Together with Fei Bao and the other three heroes, they are to carry out the plan thus, setting forth on the following day.” Li Jun received his orders and led the whole party to the shore of Lake Tai. Three men crossed the lake first, then brought boats back to ferry Li Kui and all the others to Willow Manor. Li Jun brought Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun to meet Fei Bao and his companions. When Fei Bao and the others saw Li Kui's fearsome appearance, they were all astonished. They welcomed the company of more than two hundred men and prepared wine and food for them at the manor. On the third day, after everyone had settled the plan, Fei Bao disguised himself as the chief arsenal official escorting the garments and armor, while Ni Yun posed as his deputy. Both wore the livery of the southern regime and carried the complete set of credentials and official documents. The fishermen all disguised themselves as boatmen and sailors from the government vessels, while more than two hundred officers and men, including the Black Whirlwind, hid in the holds. Bu Qing and Di Cheng took charge of the boats in the rear, carrying incendiary equipment with them. Just as they were about to set the plan in motion, another fisherman came to report: “There is a boat out on the lake, rowing back and forth.” Li Jun said, “More trouble!” He hurried out to look and saw two men standing in the bow. They proved to be Dai Zong, the Magic Messenger, and Ling Zhen, the Thunderclap. Li Jun sounded a signal whistle, and the boat sped toward the manor as though flying. When it reached the bank, the two men came ashore, and all exchanged greetings. Li Jun asked, “Where have you two come from? What news do you bring?” Dai Zong said, “Our elder brother sent Li Kui off in such haste that he forgot an important matter. He specially dispatched Ling Zhen and me to bring a hundred cannon charges aboard this boat. We could not catch you on the lake, yet dared not approach the bank here. He orders you to enter the city tomorrow at the hour of the hare. Once inside, set off these hundred fire-cannons as the signal.” Li Jun said, “Excellent!” They immediately transferred the cannon baskets and frames from the boat and concealed them all aboard the vessels carrying the garments and armor. When Fei Bao and the others learned that the visitor was Dai Zong, they again laid out wine and a feast to entertain him. The ten gunners Ling Zhen had brought were all concealed and stationed in the third boat. At the fourth watch that night they left the manor and headed for Suzhou; after the fifth watch, they reached the foot of the city walls. The soldiers guarding the gate saw the banners of the southern regime from atop the wall and hurried to inform the general in charge of the gate. This was Flying Leopard General Guo Shiguang, who came personally to the wall, questioned a junior officer in detail, received the credentials and official documents, and had them hoisted up for inspection. Guo Shiguang had the papers carried to the Third Prince's palace, where the documents were authenticated. Another man was then sent to supervise the convoy, and only afterward were the boats allowed through the city gate. Guo Shiguang remained seated beside the water gate and again sent men down to inspect the boats. Finding them packed full of iron armor and uniforms, he allowed the vessels into the city one by one. After all ten boats had passed, the water gate was closed. The supervising officer sent by the Third Prince led five hundred troops along the bank, closely following the boats, and then ordered them to moor. Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun crawled out of the holds. When the supervising officer saw the four men, all coarse and hideous in appearance, he was just about to demand who they were when Xiang Chong and Li Gun brandished their round shields. A blade flashed out, and they hacked the officer from his horse. The five hundred soldiers were about to board the boats when Li Kui raised his pair of axes, leapt ashore, and cut down more than ten of them in quick succession. The whole force of five hundred fled.

p.src: The heroes aboard the boats, together with more than two hundred shield-bearers, all came ashore and immediately began setting fires. Ling Zhen spread out his gun carriages along the bank, brought out the signal cannon, and fired more than a dozen rounds in succession. The cannon blasts shook even the city towers, and the troops attacked inward from every side. The Third Prince, Fang Mao, was holding council in his residence. Hearing the cannon fire without cease, he was so terrified that his soul nearly left his body. The commanders guarding the several gates heard the unbroken cannon fire within the city and each led his troops racing toward the center. Urgent reports came from every gate: the southern troops had all been shot dead by hidden arrows, and the Song forces had already mounted the walls. The whole city of Suzhou erupted in tumult, with no one knowing how many Song troops had entered. Li Kui the Black Whirlwind and Bao Xu led two companies of shield-bearers charging wildly through the city, hunting down and killing the southern troops. Li Jun and Dai Zong led Fei Bao and his three companions in guarding Ling Zhen, who kept firing the cannon. Song Jiang had already dispatched three columns of commanders and troops to take the city. The Song soldiers stormed into the city; the southern army scattered and fled, each man seeking to save his own life. Meanwhile, the Third Prince, Fang Mao, hastily donned his armor and mounted his horse. Leading five or seven hundred armored troops, he fought to clear a path and tried to break out through the south gate, only to run straight into Li Kui the Black Whirlwind and his band. They cut into the armored troops, sending them scrambling east and west and fleeing in every direction. Then Lu Zhishen burst from a narrow lane, swinging his iron monk's staff as he attacked. Unable to withstand him, Fang Mao spurred away alone and turned back toward his residence. From beneath Magpie Bridge came Wu Song. He caught up and slashed through the horse's legs with one stroke, throwing Fang Mao to the ground. Wu Song finished him with another blow, took his head, and went straight to headquarters to report to the vanguard commander and claim his merit. By then Song Jiang had entered the city and taken his seat in the princely residence. He ordered the commanders to search the city for the southern troops and destroy them. All were captured save Liu Yun alone, who escaped with a remnant of the defeated army and fled to Xiuzhou. A poem bears witness: The sacred realm has never brooked offense; How could a usurper king ever rest secure? Wu Song, reining in his horse, slew Fang Mao, Leaving the stubbornly wicked an example to behold.

u.src: The heroes aboard the boats, together with more than two hundred shield-bearers, all came ashore and immediately began setting fires.
Ling Zhen spread out his gun carriages along the bank, brought out the signal cannon, and fired more than a dozen rounds in succession.
The cannon blasts shook even the city towers, and the troops attacked inward from every side.
The Third Prince, Fang Mao, was holding council in his residence. Hearing the cannon fire without cease, he was so terrified that his soul nearly left his body.
The commanders guarding the several gates heard the unbroken cannon fire within the city and each led his troops racing toward the center.
Urgent reports came from every gate: the southern troops had all been shot dead by hidden arrows, and the Song forces had already mounted the walls.
The whole city of Suzhou erupted in tumult, with no one knowing how many Song troops had entered.
Li Kui the Black Whirlwind and Bao Xu led two companies of shield-bearers charging wildly through the city, hunting down and killing the southern troops.
Li Jun and Dai Zong led Fei Bao and his three companions in guarding Ling Zhen, who kept firing the cannon.
Song Jiang had already dispatched three columns of commanders and troops to take the city.
The Song soldiers stormed into the city; the southern army scattered and fled, each man seeking to save his own life.

Meanwhile, the Third Prince, Fang Mao, hastily donned his armor and mounted his horse. Leading five or seven hundred armored troops, he fought to clear a path and tried to break out through the south gate, only to run straight into Li Kui the Black Whirlwind and his band. They cut into the armored troops, sending them scrambling east and west and fleeing in every direction.
Then Lu Zhishen burst from a narrow lane, swinging his iron monk's staff as he attacked.
Unable to withstand him, Fang Mao spurred away alone and turned back toward his residence.

From beneath Magpie Bridge came Wu Song. He caught up and slashed through the horse's legs with one stroke, throwing Fang Mao to the ground. Wu Song finished him with another blow, took his head, and went straight to headquarters to report to the vanguard commander and claim his merit.

By then Song Jiang had entered the city and taken his seat in the princely residence. He ordered the commanders to search the city for the southern troops and destroy them. All were captured save Liu Yun alone, who escaped with a remnant of the defeated army and fled to Xiuzhou.
A poem bears witness: The sacred realm has never brooked offense; How could a usurper king ever rest secure?
Wu Song, reining in his horse, slew Fang Mao, Leaving the stubbornly wicked an example to behold.

p.src: Once seated in the princely residence, Song Jiang immediately issued orders that no innocent civilians were to be harmed. At the same time, he had the fires on every side extinguished, then posted proclamations of reassurance to inform soldiers and commoners alike. Afterward, the commanders assembled at the residence to report their merits. It was learned that Wu Song had killed Fang Mao; Zhu Tong had captured Xu Fang alive; Shi Jin had captured Zhen Cheng alive; Sun Li had beaten Zhang Wei to death with his whip; Li Jun had speared Chang Sheng to death; Fan Rui had killed Wu Fu; and Xuan Zan and Guo Shiguang had fought a bitter duel, each wounding the other, until both died beneath Drinking Horse Bridge. The remaining subordinate commanders had all been captured and were brought forward for the claiming of merit. When Song Jiang saw that Xuan Zan, the Ugly Commandery Prince Consort, had fallen, he mourned him without cease. He ordered a richly decorated inner and outer coffin prepared and had the body taken to the foot of Tiger Hill for burial. Fang Mao's head, together with Xu Fang and Zhen Cheng, was sent under guard to Commander Zhang's headquarters at Changzhou for judgment. Commander Zhang had Xu Fang and Zhen Cheng cut to pieces in the marketplace, while Fang Mao's head was sent on to the capital; in return, he sent many rewards to Suzhou to be distributed among the commanders. Commander Zhang submitted an official dispatch requesting that Liu Guangshi be appointed to defend Suzhou, while ordering Vanguard Commander Song to advance his troops along the way and hunt down the rebels. Presently a scout reported, “Governor Liu and Adviser Geng are coming to take charge of Suzhou.” That very day, all the commanders accompanied Vanguard Commander Song to welcome Liu Guangshi and the other officials into the city and settle them in the princely residence. When the formal greetings were over, Song Jiang and his commanders withdrew to the prefectural offices to deliberate and sent men to learn the fate of the naval leaders operating along the coast. A report soon arrived that, when the rebels in the coastal districts learned Suzhou had fallen, they had scattered and fled, and all the remote seaside counties and roads were now peaceful. Song Jiang was delighted. He sent a written victory report to headquarters, asking Commander Zhang to proclaim the reinstatement of the former officials, detach other officers from headquarters to defend each district and reassure the people, and recall the chief and deputy naval commanders and their aides to Suzhou for reassignment.

p.src: Within a few days, the commanding officers had each departed for his assigned destination. The naval leaders all returned to Suzhou and reported that the three Ruan brothers had attacked Changshu and lost Shi En, then had gone on to take Kunshan and lost Kong Liang. Shi Xiu, Li Ying, and the others had all returned, but Shi En and Kong Liang, being unable to swim, had fallen into the water in the heat of the moment and both drowned. Seeing that two more commanders had been lost, Song Jiang was deeply grieved and sighed without end. Wu Song, remembering the friendship and kindness they had shared in former days, also wept bitterly for a time.

p.src: Now Fei Bao and his three companions came to take leave of Vanguard Commander Song and return home. Song Jiang earnestly urged them to stay, but they would not. He rewarded all four generously, then ordered Li Jun to escort Fei Bao and the others back to Yuliu Manor. Li Jun, accompanied by Tong Wei and Tong Meng, escorted Fei Bao and his three companions to Yuliu Manor, where Fei Bao and the others again prepared wine and a banquet to entertain them. In the midst of the drinking, Fei Bao rose to offer Li Jun a cup and spoke a few words—words destined to make Li Jun depart the lands of the Central Plain and establish a new realm beyond the bounds of civilization. Indeed: His life fulfilled, his fate attained, the toad leaves its shell; His enterprise founded, his fame achieved, the fish becomes a dragon. What words did Fei Bao speak to Li Jun? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
